subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Single-Origin vs. Blends
description: A quick win: understand Single-Origin vs. Blends.

hook.text: English Breakfast is a blend of teas from India, Kenya, and Sri Lanka. It's designed for consistency, not terroir.

buildup.text: Blenders mix teas from many sources to hit a target flavor profile that stays the same year after year.

discovery.text: Single-origin teas vary by season and year—like wine vintages. Each harvest is unique and unrepeatable.

twist.text: Most tea drinkers prefer blends without knowing it. Consistency is comforting; terroir is adventurous.

climax.text: Both approaches have value. Blends offer reliability; single-origin offers discovery and connection to place.

punchline.text: Blends for comfort. Single-origin for exploration. Choose both.

quiz.question: Why do tea companies create blends?
options: To achieve a consistent flavor profile across seasons and years
Single-origin tea is illegal to sell

details.summary: Single-origin teas come from one garden or region, showcasing unique terroir and character. Blends combine teas from multiple sources for consistency and balance. Neither is inherently superior: single origins offer discovery and seasonality, while blends deliver reliable flavor year-round.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the single-origin versus blend distinction helps you choose tea that matches your priorities, whether that is consistency or exploration.
takeaways: Single-origin teas showcase terroir and seasonal variation
Blends prioritize consistency across batches and seasons
Most commercial tea is blended from multiple sources

faq.question: Why do tea companies blend different origins?
faq.answer: Blending maintains a consistent flavor profile that customers expect, regardless of seasonal or regional variations. A breakfast blend might use Assam for body, Kenyan for brightness, and Ceylon for balance. Blenders adjust ratios each season to maintain the target taste.

faq.question: Is single-origin tea always better quality?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Single-origin means one source, not superior quality. A low-grade single-origin can be worse than a well-crafted blend. However, the finest teas tend to be single-origin because their unique character is too distinctive to blend away.
